ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In figure (a), the amplitude-frequency curve of filter F1 has relatively high gain at low frequencies, and decreases after the frequency exceeds the cutoff frequency f1, therefore F1 behaves as a low-pass filter. In figure (b), the amplitude-frequency curve of filter F2 has relatively low gain at low frequencies, rises after approaching and exceeding the cutoff frequency f2, and passes high frequencies, therefore F2 behaves as a high-pass filter. In figure (c), the input vi is simultaneously sent into F1 and F2, and the two filtered signals then enter an operational amplifier combination network to form the output vo. Reasoning: It is known that f1 < f2. When f < f1, the F1 low-pass branch passes the signal, so the output is not zero. When f1 < f < f2, F1 has already attenuated, while F2 has not yet begun to pass effectively, therefore the outputs of both paths are very small, and the overall output is suppressed. When f > f2, the F2 high-pass branch passes the signal, so the output again is not zero. That is to say, low frequencies and high frequencies pass, and the middle frequency band is blocked, therefore the characteristic of this circuit is a band-stop filter.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: F1 is drawn with a decreasing magnitude response, so assign it a low-pass transfer H1(f); F2 is drawn with an increasing magnitude response, so assign it a high-pass transfer H2(f); circuit (c) linearly combines these two filtered versions of the same input. Model the output as Vo = a H1(f)Vi + b H2(f)Vi, where a and b are nonzero constants determined by the op-amp resistors/signs. From the text, f1 < f2. Thus H1 is appreciable mainly for f < f1, H2 is appreciable mainly for f > f2, and both are small in the interval f1 < f < f2. Therefore the weighted sum has transmission at low and high frequencies but attenuation in the intermediate band, so the resultant circuit is a band-stop filter.
